subject: Career
title: Meeting Politics: Who Speaks, Who Listens
description: A fast breakdown of Meeting Politics: Who Speaks, Who Listens for builders.

hook.text: In a meeting of ten, three people do 70% of the talking. Those three shape the outcome.

buildup.text: Meetings are political arenas disguised as collaborative spaces. Airtime equals influence.

discovery.text: Seating position matters: people near the facilitator speak more. People at the end speak least.

twist.text: Women and minorities speak 25% less in mixed meetings. Their ideas get attributed to louder voices.

climax.text: Counter this: use round-robins, pre-read docs, and written input to equalize participation.

punchline.text: Meetings aren't neutral. Design them or the loudest voice wins.

quiz.question: What percentage of meeting talk is typically dominated by a few people?
options: Three people do about 70% of the talking

details.summary: Meetings are political arenas where speaking order, interruptions, and silence all carry meaning. Who gets airtime, whose ideas get built upon, and who gets ignored reveal the true power dynamics of any team or organization.
details.whyItMatters: Most professionals spend significant time in meetings. Understanding meeting politics helps you gain influence, protect your ideas, and read organizational dynamics accurately.
takeaways: The first person to speak often frames the entire discussion
Interruption patterns reveal informal hierarchy regardless of titles
Building on others' ideas with attribution builds political goodwill

faq.question: How do you get your ideas heard in meetings dominated by loud voices?
faq.answer: Pre-meeting preparation is key. Share your position with key stakeholders before the meeting so they arrive already aligned with your view. In the meeting, use concise language and a confident tone. If interrupted, calmly say 'I would like to finish my point' and continue.

faq.question: What does it mean politically when you are consistently excluded from meetings?
faq.answer: Exclusion from relevant meetings signals marginalization in the power structure. Address it directly by asking your manager why you are not included and framing your presence as adding value to the discussion rather than requesting a favor.
